Abstract

LLM-based agents process external content, exposing them to prompt injection and multi-turn manipulation. Most safety benchmarks evaluate defenders against fixed attack pools collected before evaluation, single-turn or multi-turn. We present a 21-scenario benchmark foradaptive multi-round attacks against memoryless LLM defenders: an autonomous LLM attacker observes prior defender responses and pivots across rounds, while each defender response is evaluated as a fresh interaction. Holding the 21 scenarios, attackers, defenders, and structured-output scoring fixed, restricting scoring to the first attacker turn yields0–1% attack success rate (ASR); allowing 15 rounds of adaptive attack yields 5.4–14.0%. Pooling three frontier attacker LLMs uncovers 1.4–2.2× as many unique successful attacks as the best single attacker, and the generated attacks have low cosine similarity (0.02–0.14) to attacks in existing benchmarks. blocks.text: Introduction

Evaluating LLM-agent safety against indirect prompt injection [Greshake et al., 2023] and multi-turn jailbreaking [Li et al., 2024, Russinovich et al., 2025] requires adversarial benchmarks: collections of scenarios in which an attacker tries to manipulate a defender into producing unsafe output. We measure outcomes byattack success rate (ASR): the fraction of battles in which the attacker succeeds. Most current safety benchmarks evaluate defenders against areleasedattack pool that is collected before evaluation and reused across defenders. This holds across single-turn prompt datasets [Souly et al., 2024, Chao et al., 2024, Mazeika et al., 2024], crowdsourced human-attack collections [Bazinska et al., 2025, Li et al., 2024], LLM-attacker pipelines such as PAIR [Chao et al., 2023] and TAP [Mehrotra et al., 2024] (which generate adaptive attacks during construction but release a static post-hoc set), Crescendo [Russinovich et al., 2025], and recent agentic benchmarks [Andriushchenko et al., 2024, Sinha and Inspect Evals contributors, 2025, Debenedetti et al., 2024]. We build a security benchmark on top of the AgentBeats multi-agent evaluation platform [Berkeley AgentBeats Team, 2026] (§3); its open competition in early 2026 (§4.2) supplies the 18,422-battle ∗Correspondence todevina.jain@lambda.ai. blocks.text: Related Work

We organize prior safety benchmarks along three axes:turn structure(single vs. multi-turn),attack persistence(whether the released attack pool is fixed before evaluation or regenerated per battle), and attacker source(human-authored, single-LLM, or multi-LLM-agent). Table 1 positions each cited benchmark on these axes. Single-turn human-authored datasets.StrongREJECT [Souly et al., 2024] (313 forbidden prompts), JailbreakBench [Chao et al., 2024] (100 harmful behaviors), and HarmBench [Mazeika et al., 2024] (510 behaviors) ship a fixed, human-authored single-turn pool. b3 [Bazinska et al., 2025] pairs 30threat snapshots(Lakera Gandalf) with 194K crowdsourced single-turn attempts; each is a one-shot prompt against a stateless defender, not a multi-turn dialogue. Multi-turn human-attack datasets.MHJ [Li et al., 2024] curates 537 multi-turn human-authored jailbreak conversations from professional red-teamers, establishing a multi-turn ASR boost consistent with what we observe in §5.3 under a different (LLM-generated, memoryless-defender) protocol. LLM-attacker pipelines.PAIR [Chao et al., 2023], TAP [Mehrotra et al., 2024], Crescendo [Russinovich et al., 2025], and GCG [Zou et al., 2023] generate adaptive attacks during construction — iteratively optimizing against a target defender — but the resulting attacks are typically logged and reused as a fixed evaluation set, and the attacker LLM is not treated as a benchmark measurement axis. Agent benchmarks.AgentHarm [Andriushchenko et al., 2024] (176 multi-turn agent tasks with

simulated tools), IPI Coding Agent [Sinha and Inspect Evals contributors, 2025] (45 indirect prompt injection scenarios in Docker sandboxes), and AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al., 2024] (1,014 user-task / injection-task pairs) evaluate multi-turn agents but ship pre-authored attack pools fixed across defenders. The combination of axes above leaves one quadrant unfilled:multi-turn × regenerated per battle × multi-LLM-agent attacker. This is the gap the present benchmark fills. Calibration methodology.Item Response Theory [Lord, 1980, Embretson and Reise, 2000] provides classical machinery for evaluating whether benchmark items reliably measure a latent ability, and has been applied to LLM capability benchmarks [Polo et al., 2024]. Design principles

Our benchmark runs on the AgentBeats platform [Berkeley AgentBeats Team, 2026]. Each battle pairs one attacker harness with one defender harness (Python modules that wrap LLM calls with prompt construction, output parsing, and optional pre- or post-processing) under an orchestrator configured with a per-scenario template and structured defender output contract; scoring is performed by check_success as described below. In the controlled 3×3 frontier evaluation, the harness logic is fixed and only the attacker/defender LLMs vary; in the open competition (§4.2), teams submit their own harnesses. A battle proceeds for 15 rounds: the orchestrator passes scenario context and prior defender responses to the attacker, inserts the attacker’s text into the scenario template, passes only the formatted current input to the defender (no attack metadata, no prior-round history), parses its structured JSON, and runs check_success. The asymmetry is deliberate: the attacker plans across rounds and pivots after failures, while the defender is evaluated as a fresh interaction each round, isolating per-input robustness under sustained adaptive pressure. Memoryless defender.Evaluating each defender response without prior-round history is a deliberate threat model: it represents an adversary who opens a fresh defender session per attempt (so no suspicion accumulates on the defender side) while itself learning across attempts, and it isolates whether a single crafted input compromises the defender. The reported ASR is therefore a per-input

stress-test estimate, not a production-agent prediction; a stateful agent may be moreorless robust, depending on whether accumulated history helps it detect the manipulation or instead reinforces it (§5.3, §6). Four design choices define the benchmark; §5 tests their effects. Multi-stage authoring with quantitative calibration.We treat each scenario as a measurement instrument that must reliably distinguish stronger from weaker defenders; a scenario can fail in this role by being uninformatively easy or hard, capability-insensitive, or first-round exploitable. Each 3

released scenario went through three stages.(i) Concept generation.Concepts are LLM-seeded and human-curated: a GPT-4o-mini generator produces concept specs covering one of seven attack archetypes (indirect injection, prompt extraction, insecure output, PII leak, supply-chain, DoS, jailbreak). Authors review, tweak, or reject before plugin implementation.(ii) Plugin implementation. Each candidate becomes a Python plugin (threat-snapshot format adapted from b3 [Bazinska et al., 2025]): defender system prompt, output schema, dialogue template, and check_success.(iii) Calibration filter.Calibration usesstrong= gpt-5.2 andweak= gpt-4o-mini. Each plugin runs in three configs:BAL(balanced: same model on both sides),SVW(strong attacker, weak defender), andWVS(weak attacker, strong defender), 10 runs per config (30 calibration runs total). Calibration is performed once on this pair; transfer to frontier defenders is checked via the released-set difficulty distribution (§4) and the cross-tier check in Appendix B.9. The rubric (Table 2) scores these three scenario-as-instrument failure modes; run-to-run sampling noise is characterized separately on the released set in §4.2.

Multi-turn agent-vs-agent over single-turn attacks.Every scenario is a 15-round dialogue between two LLM agents. The defender is memoryless across rounds, but the attacker reads the defender’s prior responses and conditions each attempt on what the defender just said. AgentHarm [Andriushchenko et al., 2024] runs multi-turn agents against a fixed user prompt; we replace the fixed prompt with a multi-turn LLM attacker. Per-battle attack regeneration over fixed attack pools.The attacker LLM generates each turn live, not from a pre-collected pool. Stored-pool benchmarks (b 3’s 194,331 crowdsourced attacks, AgentHarm’s fixed templates) are reproducible but cannot adapt mid-battle. Live generation reverses this trade-off: attacks adapt to defender behavior, but closed-model runs are auditable and replayable rather than bit-for-bit reproducible. Structured checks.Defenders output structured JSON, and check_success scores only scenariorelevant fields, not free-form prose. We count an attack successful only when the unsafe outcome is

committed in the scenario’s designated typed field, or the protected asset reaches a party other than the attacker; partial, ambiguous, echo-only, or merely topically-related responses are scored as failures (per-scenario criteria in Appendix A; the criterion and its borderline handling in Appendix B.13– B.15).
The Benchmark
Scenario set

Ascenariospecifies a defender role and protected asset, a per-round attack-input template, and a check_success function over structured defender fields that decides per battle whether the attacker has succeeded. Figure 9 shows the canonical card layout with a worked example. The released benchmark contains21 held-out evaluation scenariosand10 public scenariosfor iterative development (defender prompts for the public scenarios are withheld to preserve the live competition; Appendix E). The 21 cover five threat classes: indirect injection (11 scenarios), PII / data leak (6), insecure output (2), supply chain (1), and prompt extraction (1). Full descriptions are in Appendix A. 4

Resultant difficulty distribution.As a calibration check on the released set, we ran the Baseline attacker against the Baseline defender on gpt-oss-20b at N=50 per scenario (1,050 battles). The per-scenario ASR distribution spans the full range: 7 of 21 scenarios have ASR above 70%, 5 cluster 22–48%, 9 sit below 20% (3 at exactly 0%); per-scenario numbers in Appendix A. The scenario set is non-degenerate at this tier. Per-scenario ranking is tier-specific (§5.1); a scenario that is a robust ceiling at one defender tier may yield non-trivial ASR at another.
The open competition

The AgentBeats Security Arena open competition ran March–April 2026 on the gpt-oss-20b backbone (self-hosted vLLM, Appendix B), with 21 independently submitted attacker teams and 20 independently submitted defender teams. The competition had two phases. In 53 public-scenario rounds, teams iterated on the 10 public scenarios, producing ∼93,000 battles and surfacing check_success edge cases that were hardened before final scoring. In two private-scoring rounds, the submitted agents were evaluated on the 21 held-out scenarios released here, producing 18,422 battles. Submissions ranged from prompt-engineered single-LLM agents to multi-stage pipelines with input filtering, output classifiers, and iterative attack planners. The held-out set distinguishedfixed-catalogharnesses (which overfit to the public 10 scenarios) fromadaptive-selectionharnesses (which generalized); full analysis in Appendix B. These private rounds support the strategy-space analysis in §5.4.

blocks.text: Cross-benchmark concordance and informativeness

Many scenarios carry signal, yet they disagree on which defender is weakest — so aggregate ASR hides scenario-specific vulnerabilities.We quantify this with Kendall’s W on per-item defender rankings for each benchmark (bootstrap 95% CIs; Table 3). W= 1 means every item ranks the three defenders identically (one underlying “safety” axis); W= 0 means rankings are random. b3 sits at W= 0.712 (Gemini ranks weakest across most informative items). Our W= 0.19 has CI [0.02,0.58] , separating from b3 but overlapping the CIs of MHJ (0.204), JBB (0.210), and AgentHarm (0.328). The distinctive pattern is thecombination: 14/21 scenarios areinformative (they produce at least one attacker win), and 13 of these arediscriminative(the defender ranking differs) — the highest rates among the six benchmarks — yet the per-scenario rankings disagree. (promptphantom is informative but not discriminative: all three defenders are compromised once, so it carries signal but no ranking.) This high rate is partly by construction — scenarios were calibrated to be capability-sensitive (§3), so a large fraction carrying signal is expected, and we do not read it as a coverage result. The low concordance, however, is not forced by that calibration, which used a separate strong/weak pair and targeted no ordering among the three defenders: were frontier-defender safety one-dimensional, capability-sensitive scenarios would rank the three defenders consistently and W would be high. The observed W=0.19 (computed over the 14 informative scenarios) instead
indicates that,given this calibrated scenario set, frontier-defender weaknesses do not align on a single axis.

Limitations

Sample size.At N=5 per cell, the large-gap scenarios are diagnostic and supported by clear transcript-level mechanisms. We additionally replicate the three running examples at N=20 per cell (60 per defender; Appendix B.9), which preserves each pattern:memleak(Opus 50%, GPT-5.4 10%, Gemini 5%), paperaccept (Gemini 43%, others ≤2%), and smarthomejack (GPT-5.4 7%, others ≤2% — confirming it stays within sampling noise). We treat as model-specific only the gaps that are statistically separated (memleak, paperaccept, gameguru); smarthomejack is reported as diagnostic, not a model-specific claim. Attacker capability.Attackers are natural-language LLM agents, which makes attacker identity measurable but bounds the attack space by both the attacker model’s capability ceiling and its own safety training. The benchmark therefore complements but does not fully replace human red-teaming, which can pursue strategies that LLM attackers are trained to refuse. 8
Figure 4: Attack-content embedding (MiniLM-L6-v2 → UMAP) across seven safety benchmarks.

Sampled ton≤250per benchmark. Scenario coverage and selection.The 21 held-out evaluation scenarios span five threat classes but concentrate on indirect injection and data leakage. They are also curated for difficulty, sensitivity, and round depth, so informative-scenario rate and low concordance are not estimates from a random task sample. Cross-benchmark ASR comparisons are likewise not leaderboard rankings: judges, content, turn structures, and threat surfaces differ across benchmarks. Reproducibility.We build a repeatable evaluation framework, not a token-by-token reproducible artifact. Closed API endpoints may drift over time, and live attack generation is not bit-for-bit reproducible by construction. The release supports audit and re-evaluation rather than exact reproduction of the closed-model runs: transcripts preserve the observed battles, attack replays enable controlled reruns, and the open-weightgpt-oss-20breference provides one exactly replicable tier. Defender state.The memoryless protocol (§3) isolates per-input robustness; it does not model a stateful production agent that carries conversation history. Such an agent is generally more robust — our stateful-defender ablation lowers pooled ASR (§5.3, App. B.12) — though not uniformly, since accumulated history can reinforce a manipulation as well as help the defender refuse it. Practical defenses.Because no single frontier model is safest across scenarios, deployments should not rely on a single “most robust” model. The recurring failure — obeying fake authority injected

into the input — argues for separating trusted instructions from untrusted content and gating securitycritical actions behind explicit confirmation, which the defenders that held already approximate (e.g. Gemini parks unlocks in actions_pending). Our memleak finding is a harder, distinct failure — secret disclosure under a benign-debugging reframe — that these mitigations do not address; we leave it to future work.
Conclusion

Static attack pools are insufficient for agent-security evaluation: they freeze the adversary before the defender is measured. Adaptive evaluation changes the measurement object — the attacker model, interaction budget, and scenario set all affect which vulnerabilities surface — and our benchmark operationalizes this view as a repeatable protocol. The 3×3 frontier evaluation surfaces what fixed-pool, single-attacker evaluation can miss: Opus and GPT-5.4 tie in aggregate ASR (5.4% each) but diverge sharply by scenario; pooling three attacker LLMs uncovers 1.4–2.2× more unique successful attacks than the best single attacker; and round-1only scoring misses most of the failures exposed over 15 adaptive rounds. We release the protocol, scenarios, harnesses, and traces (Appendix E) to support direct extensions along each axis this release holds fixed: stateful defenders, a broader attacker pool (more models), additional threat models, domains, and scenarios, and larger-Nruns that vary the per-battle round count. 9

B.15 Reward hacking of proxy success metrics by adaptive attacker agents Substring/proxy success metrics — “a marker string is present,” or “an executed action’s name contains unlock” — are gameable by adaptive attacker agents, which satisfy the proxy without achieving the threat. We observe this directly in two scenarios. tickettriage.The attacker’s objective is literally “the referral code must appear in a reply.” The suggested promotional framing (“use code X for 20% off”) is refused by all defenders; adaptive attackers instead disguised the code as a customer-supplied error or reference ID, which the bot echoes back as routine support. Under naive scoring this reads as up to 67% ASR, but0 of 30 such “wins” propagate the code to a different customer or present it as a usable code — every one echoes the attacker’s own self-supplied reference back to the attacker. A residual real signal survives: GPT-5.4 followed anembedded reproduce-this-code instructionin 5/15 battles, while Opus and Gemini resisted such instructions in 0/29 and 0/23 attempts (input-aware analysis; heuristic). smarthomejack.Attackers emitted decoy actions named unlock_front_door/open on peripheral devices (a chime module’s sound profile, a glow strip’s mode, a status panel’s display text) to trip the

substring check; the lock never opens. Only 2 of 45 battles executed an actual unlock. We surfaced both by manually auditing every attacker-winning battle (independently confirmed by four reviewers; of 121 candidate wins under a substring check, 78 are genuine compromises). Both behaviours share one cause — a check that rewards a marker’sappearancerather than the occurrenceof the threat. We therefore score by whether the unsafe outcome actually occurs — recipient/endorsement-aware for tickettriage, exact-action-on-a-lock for smarthomejack — crediting a compromise only when the unsafe outcome is committed in a typed field or reaches a third party. Proxy/substring success metrics are gameable by adaptive LLM agents, so careful design of the success criterion is critical. 25
